blocks.text: III. To the third question, from where these quails came, Moses answers in Num. XI, 31. that a wind, proceeding from the Lord, brought them מן הים, from the sea. And the author of the book of Wisdom, chapter 19, verse 12: For their comfort the ortygometra came up to them from the sea. Some have taken this as though they had been born in the sea itself. I see that some of the Arabs hold this opinion. The same Assariph as above: سماني هو طاير يخرج من البحر [samānī huwa ṭāyir yakhruj min al-baḥr] The quail is a bird that comes out of the sea. Damir: وهو من الطيور القواطع لا يدري من اين يابي حتي ان بعض الناس يقول انه يخرج من البحر المالح فانه يري طاير عليه واحد جناحية فيه منغمس والاخر منشور كالقلع والاهل مصر به عنايه ويتغالون في ثمنه [wa-huwa min al-ṭuyūr al-qawāṭiʿ lā yudrā min ayna yābī ḥattā anna baʿḍ al-nās yaqūl annahu yakhruj min al-baḥr al-māliḥ fa-innahu yurā ṭāyir ʿalayhi wāḥid janāḥiyya fīhi munghamis wa-al-ākhar manshūr ka-al-qilʿ wa-al-ahl miṣr bihi ʿināya wa-yataghālūn fī thamanihi] It is one of the migratory birds, and it is so unknown where it comes from that some assert that it comes out of the salt sea and is seen flying over it, with one of its wings immersed and the other spread out like a sail. The Egyptians are very keen on it, and therefore hold this bird to be precious. Nor does Aben Ezra seem to have meant anything else when, on the words of Moses in Exod. XVI, 13, And the quail came up and covered the camp, he added this little note: אולי עלתה מפאת ים, Perhaps it had come up from the region of the sea. And among the Greeks, Phanodemus is thought to have held the same view, when he wrote in his Atthis that Delos was called Ortygia by the ancients, that is, the island of quails, παρὰ τὰς ἀγέλας τῶν ζώων τούτων, φερομένας ἐκ τοῦ πελάγους, ἱζάνειν εἰς τὴν νῆσον διὰ τὸ εὔορμον εἶναι [para tas agelas tōn zōōn toutōn, pheromenas ek tou pelagous, hizanein eis tēn nēson dia to euormon einai], because many flocks of these creatures, [II, 661] borne from the sea, settle on that island, since it is a convenient resting place. And Kiranides, in book 1, talks nonsense: that from tunnies cast up on the shore of Libya, as they rot, worms are born which have first the form and size of flies, then of locusts, and finally of quails. But whatever they thought, it is certain that quails are born and feed on bare ground. The Sacred Writer therefore writes that they came from the sea in the sense in which Pliny, book 10, ch. 29, said: A great number of wood pigeons flies every year from the sea into the territory of Volaterrae. Not that they are produced in it, but that, having crossed it, they betake themselves to the area around Volaterrae. So, then, the wind is said to have brought the quails from the sea because, having crossed the Arabian sea, it had carried them from Egypt into the camp of the Israelites. To this belong these words of Josephus, Antiqu. book 3, ch. 1: Καὶ μετ᾽ ὀλίγον ὀρτύγων πλῆθος· τρέφει δὲ τοῦτο τὸ ὄρνεον, ὡς οὐδὲν ἕτερον, ὁ Ἀράβιος κόλπος, ἐπίπταται τὴν μεταξὺ θάλασσαν ὑπερελθόν [Kai met' oligon ortygōn plēthos; trephei de touto to orneon, hōs ouden heteron, ho Arabios kolpos, epiptatai tēn metaxy thalassan hyperelthon]. And shortly afterwards a great number of quails flew in, having crossed the intervening sea; for the Arabian gulf nourishes this kind of bird more than any other. Not far from there is Rhinocolura, where, as Diodorus reports in book 1, page 38, a great number of quails flying in from the sea is caught, in these words: Καλάμην γὰρ κείροντες ἐκ τῆς ὁμόρου χώρας, καὶ ταύτην σχίζοντες λίνα παραμήκη κατασκεύαζον. ταῦτα δὲ παρὰ τὸν αἰγιαλὸν ἐπὶ πολλοὺς σταδίους ἱστάντες τὰς θήρας τῶν ὀρτύγων ἐποιοῦντο (φέρονται γὰρ οὗτοι κατ᾽ ἀγέλας μείζους ἐκ τοῦ πελάγους) οὓς θηρεύοντες ἤθροιζον πλῆθος ἱκανὸν εἰς διατροφὴν [col. 101] ἑαυτοῖς· [Kalamēn gar keirontes ek tēs homorou chōras, kai tautēn schizontes lina paramēkē kateskeuazon. tauta de para ton aigialon epi pollous stadious histantes tas thēras tōn ortygōn epoiounto (pherontai gar houtoi kat' agelas meizous ek tou pelagous) hous thēreuontes ēthroizon plēthos hikanon eis diatrophēn heautois] Cutting reeds from the neighbouring region and splitting them, they made long nets; setting these up near the shore over many stadia, they caught the quails, which betake themselves there in great flocks from the sea, and gathered as many of them as sufficed for their sustenance. Here it should be noted that he says the quails φέρεσθαι ἐκ τοῦ πελάγους [pheresthai ek tou pelagous], just as Moses above.

These things, indeed, are obvious enough. But no one could easily say how they are to be reconciled with these words of David on the same miracle, Psal. LXXVIII, 26. 27.^{(3)} He stirred up the east wind in the heaven, and by his power drove on the south wind, and rained flesh upon them like dust, and winged birds like the sand of the sea. For what need was there for the east wind to be stirred up so that quails might be carried from Egypt into Arabia across the Arabian gulf, when this would rather be the task of Favonius and the western winds? For with respect to Egypt and Africa, the east wind does not blow into Arabia but blows out of Arabia, according to the line of the Poet:
The east wind withdrew to the Dawn and the Nabataean realms.
